sources.entry: Intel Xeon Processor Scalable Family Technical Overview - Where Intel names the mesh, UPI socket links, the directory-running home agent, and how SNC splits the cache.

summary.title: Intel® Xeon® Processor Scalable Family Technical Overview
summary.one_liner: Learn how Intel's Skylake-SP Xeon Scalable generation changed the on-chip interconnect (mesh), inter-socket links (UPI), cache hierarchy, sub-NUMA clustering, directory coherency, and AVX-512.
takeaways: Skylake-SP replaced the ring interconnect with a mesh where each core and LLC slice has a combined Caching and Home Agent (CHA).
Intel UPI replaced QPI, uses a directory-based home snoop protocol, and runs up to 10.4 GT/s with two or three links per processor.
The LLC became non-inclusive with a 1 MB MLC per core, so a snoop filter is needed to track private-cache lines.
Sub-NUMA clustering splits each socket into two localization domains; only directory snoop mode is supported.
AVX-512 adds AVX512DQ, AVX512BW and AVX512VL, extending 512-bit operations and allowing vector length down to 128 or 256 bits.
summary.summary: This Intel developer article is a technical overview of the Xeon Scalable processor family (Skylake-SP, 14nm, Purley platform) compared with the prior Broadwell-EP generation. It explains the move from a ring to a mesh interconnect with distributed CHAs, the Intel UPI socket links and their directory-based coherency, and how sub-NUMA clustering and the non-inclusive cache hierarchy change latency and capacity behavior. It also covers security and ISA features such as protection keys, Intel MPX, mode-based execute, and the AVX-512 subsets.
